extracted.intended_audience: War Department officials, military administrators, and lawyers handling military discharges and personnel/records issues
extracted.subtask_description: Authoritative compilation of legal holdings and administrative standards governing discharge certificates, types of discharge, correction/issuance/recall of discharge instruments, and the powers of military and civil authorities with respect to separations from the U.S. military service. Intended to guide officials and counsel in deciding and documenting discharge status and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: I F. Muster-out rule during Civil and Spanish Wars
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Civil and Spanish Wars there was a rule, published in general orders, to the effect that when Volunteer troops are mustered out of service the entire regiment or other organization will be considered as having been mustered out at the same time and place, except prisoners of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that this did not include deserters at large who had been dropped from the rolls. C. 10141, Apr. 3, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV A 1. Legal effect of formal certificate of discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal certificate of discharge, signed as required by the fourth article of war and furnished the soldier is legal evidence of the fact of discharge and of the circumstances, when stated, under which it was given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is furnished the soldier primarily for his use, but not being a record, the statements therein are not conclusive upon the Government when contradicted by record or better evidence. (Cited cases.) Also: an entry on a certificate of discharge of the date of enlistment is a copy from the original record and if erroneous may be corrected by the War Department by substituting a new and correct certificate or by indorsing a statement on the old certificate; the discharge is complete without the final statements. (P. 51, 126, Dec. 1891; other citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV A 2. Effect of disbandment on deserter status and power to discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: While a Volunteer soldier was absent in desertion, the Volunteer Armies were disbanded under an act of Congress. Held that the soldier upon the disbandment ceased, by operation of law, to be a deserter and became a civilian; that his military record, so far as the War Department was concerned, ended with the proper entry of the fact of his desertion; that in the absence of statutory authority the War Department was without power to legally discharge the soldier after the Volunteer Armies by disbandment ceased to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the party was in fact discharged, actually or constructively, before or at the time the Volunteer forces were disbanded, as shown by the records, a certificate to that effect could at any time be given by the War Department. (Multiple citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV A 3. Who may sign a soldier's discharge certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: A commanding officer who is not in the same regiment as the soldier will sign the discharge certificate of a soldier under his command only when no field officer of the enlisted man's regiment is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV A 4. Entitlement to discharge certificates under Feb. 24, 1897 act
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of February 24, 1897 (29 Stat., 593), was to provide for the relief of certain officers and enlisted men of the volunteer forces during the Civil War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that those who were beneficiaries under that act were entitled to have discharge certificates furnished them. C. 3021, Mar. 19, 1897.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV A 5. Completing defective discharge certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: A discharge certificate in favor of a volunteer soldier which was subsequently found to be defective in that it had not been signed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the certificate could later be completed by signature. C. 10889, July 26, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV B 1. Issuing discharge certificate under assumed names relief act
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of April 14, 1890 (26 Stat. 55), entitled 'An act for the relief of soldiers and sailors who enlisted or served under assumed names ... during the Civil War'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that a son of a slave, originally enlisted under the name of his former master and discharged as such in 1864, might legally have a discharge certificate issued to him in the name of his father, who had been given his freedom since the enlistment of his son. P. 60, 354, July, 1893.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV B 2. Replacing certificates impaired by erroneous entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a certificate of honorable discharge has had its value impaired by a later erroneous entry thereon,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that there was no legal objection to an issue by the War Department of a new certificate containing no reference to the erroneous entry. P. 34, 222, Aug., 1889; citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV B 3. Furnishing certified copy when original is not parchment
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier was discharged in Alaska and given a discharge certificate, not on parchment but on paper. He applied for a parchment certificate of discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that he is not then in the service and cannot therefore be given a discharge therefrom, but that no legal objection is seen to furnishing him a certified copy of the manuscript discharge made up on the parchment form and retaining the original in The Adjutant General's Office. C. 6982, Sept. 8, 1899; 6983, Sept. 12, 1899.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV B 4. Limits on duplicate issuance under section 224, R.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 224, R. S., does not authorize the Secretary of War to issue a duplicate certificate of discharge to replace one lost, to an officer or soldier who served in the Mexican War, or to one who served in any war other than 'the late war against the rebellion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV C 1. Secretary of War's discretion to re-issue lost duplicate certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a duplicate certificate, having been furnished, has been lost or destroyed,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that as the statute does not prohibit the issuing of a second certificate, the Secretary of War may, under the power which, as representative of the President is vested in him, issue such certificate if in his judgment it is proper to do so. C. 3101, Apr., 1897; 12029, Feb. 15, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV D 1. Entitlement to certificate of service upon proof of loss
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who had served during the Spanish War requested a certificate of service; Held that under the Army Regulations he was entitled to such a certificate which should show the date of enlistment and discharge from the Army and character given on discharge, upon proof of the loss of the original certificate or of its destruction without the fault of the party entitled to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also held that under the same regulations and independently of section 224, R. S., a 'certificate of service,' substantially in accordance with the form referred to above, should be issued to a soldier of any war or to his heirs, upon satisfactory proof of the loss or destruction of the original certificate of discharge. C. 7114, Sept. 30, 1899; 13037, July 29, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV D 2. Destruction by accident qualifies for certificate of service
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier's dishonorable discharge was rendered illegible by his being 'upset from a boat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the certificate was destroyed within the meaning of the act of July 1, 1902 (32 Stat. 629), and that he was entitled to a certificate of service. C. 14131, Feb. 12, 1903.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV D 3. Absence without leave at muster-out date — civilian status and certificate of service
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier of the Thirty-second Infantry, United States Volunteers, absented himself without leave at Nagasaki, Japan, when the transport carrying the regiment to the United States for muster out stopped at that port. He had not reported for duty when the regiment was mustered out, and was carried on the roll as absent without leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that he was legally chargeable with notice of his muster out as of the date on which his regiment was mustered out, and upon that date he legally became a civilian, and not being in the military service can not be given a discharge therefrom as requested. Held further that there is no legal objection to giving him a certificate of service, setting forth the facts that he passed out of the military service on date of the muster out of his company, being at that date absent without leave. C. 12464, July 8, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV D 4. Medical cadets and certificate of service under July 1, 1902 act
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 of the act of August 3, 1861 authorized the enlistment of 'medical cadets.' One of them lost his discharge certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held, that as he was an enlisted man a certificate of service under the act of July 1, 1902 (32 Stat. 629), could be furnished to him. C. 21108, Feb. 23, 1907.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIV D 5. Correcting discharge-without-honor issued by mistake of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier was granted a discharge without honor under a mistake as to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the corrected statement of facts could be entered by the War Department on the discharge certificate and the certificate returned to the man, or, preferably, the corrected discharge-without-honor certificate could be retained by the War Department and a certificate of service, showing the correct statement of facts, furnished to the man. C. 11741, Jan. 30, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: XV A. Finality of executed honorable discharges (fraud exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: An executed honorable discharge issued by competent authority cannot be revoked unless obtained by fraud on the part of the soldier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere mistake on the part of the officers executing it will not justify revocation. The same is equally true of a discharge without honor when once duly executed. (Multiple citations.) O. 26092, Jan. 18, 1910; other citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: XV A 1. Delivery of certificate can effect discharge absent fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Case where discharge certificate and final statements were made out and handed to a soldier who thereafter considered himself a free man and secured employment as a civilian; he was later arrested as a deserter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that no fraud had been practiced in the securing of his discharge and that he was actually discharged from the service when the discharge certificate was handed him by the sergeant major. C. 15581, Mar. 28, 1908; other citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: XV A 2. Orders attempting to change an executed honorable discharge are inoperative
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer secured a commission in the volunteer service by fraud and was honorably discharged when his regiment was mustered out. Later, a War Department order was issued which purported to dishonorably discharge him as of the date of his muster out on account of irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the order which purported to change the honorable discharge to a dishonorable one was inoperative. C. 9121, Oct. 13, 1900, and Aug. 17, 1906.

rubrics_metrics.name: XV B. Finality of duly executed dishonorable discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier has been legally sentenced to be dishonorably discharged and such discharge issued by competent authority has been duly executed, it is beyond the power of the Executive, whatever the merits of the case, to substitute an honorable one in lieu of the dishonorable discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The latter having gone into effect cannot be undone; moreover, the soldier having been thereby wholly detached from the military service and made a civilian, cannot again be discharged from the service until he has been again enlisted into it. (Multiple citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XV C. Discharge without honor, once executed, not revocable
rubrics_metrics.description: A man was legally discharged without honor by competent authority under a mistake as to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the discharge was not revocable. (Cited cases; see also Discharge XV A.) C. 1876, Nov. 25, 1895; 2099, Mar. 4, 1896; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: XV C 1. Discharge executed during confinement is final even if sentence illegal
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier was serving sentence at expiration of term of enlistment and a discharge without honor was delivered to his commanding officer. Before the expiration of his sentence the sentence was discovered to be illegal and was declared void, and the man ordered released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the discharge had been legally executed and could not be revoked, and that it should be delivered to the man upon his release from confinement. C. 13210, Aug. 29, 1902; 13209, Aug. 30, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: XV D 1. Unauthorized revocation or substitution of executed discharges illegal
rubrics_metrics.description: An order purporting to revoke a legally executed honorable discharge, not obtained by fraud, and substituting therefor a dishonorable one, held wholly unauthorized and illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly held regarding orders purporting to substitute an honorable discharge for a legally executed discharge without honor, or a legally executed dishonorable discharge. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XV D 1 a. Mistake of fact in order does not invalidate a duly executed discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier was duly discharged pursuant to an order from the War Department. The order was issued under a misapprehension in regard to his actual status at the time — a mistake of fact, which if discovered would have deferred or prevented the issuing of the order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the mistake of fact did not invalidate the discharge; that having been duly executed, it could not be revoked. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XV D 1 b. Discharge given while charges pending (unknown to discharging authority) is final
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier, before the expiration of his term, received under the fourth article of war a discharge in due form, though charges were then pending against him, the authority ordering the discharge not having been made aware of such charges,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the discharge was executed and could not be revoked with a view to bringing the soldier to trial; that he had, by the discharge, duly become a civilian. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XV Die. Notation of error of fact on records/certificate if soldier desires
rubrics_metrics.description: Through an error of fact a discharge without honor was given to a soldier;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that a notation showing this may be made on the records and also on the certificate of discharge if the soldier so desires. C. 6358, May 15, 1899; 11741, Jan. 11, 1902; 14820, June 18, 1903.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI A 1. Escrow discharges obtained by fraud do not separate soldier from service
rubrics_metrics.description: General Orders 108 provided that discharge certificates should be prepared for enlisted men who were absent for proper and sufficient reasons, and that these should be held in escrow by the company or organization commander and delivered when the conditions of the escrow had been fulfilled. A discharge was made out and so held in escrow in the case of a soldier who was absent in desertion. He later, through fraud, secured possession of this discharge certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that as this honorable discharge was obtained by fraud and could have been obtained in no other way, it did not operate to separate the claimant from the military service on the date and for the cause set forth in the discharge certificate. C. 20529, Oct. 24, 1906; 1791, Jan. 2, 1896.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI A 2. Conditional discharges secured by agreement (reenlistment) may be revoked if conditions broken
rubrics_metrics.description: An honorable discharge of a soldier was authorized in advance of the expiration of his term on condition that he should reenlist immediately for service in the Philippine Islands. He was accordingly honorably discharged. He failed to reenlist and thus repudiated the agreement with the United States, in the operation of which his honorable discharge had been secured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that his discharge had been obtained by fraud and that it was not binding upon the Government and might be repudiated and set aside by the Secretary of War; the discharge was actually ordered set aside and a new discharge without honor of a different and later date was issued in its place. C. 15581, Dec. 8, 1903, and Mar. 28, 1908; 20529, Oct. 24, 1906.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI A 3. Fraudulent alteration inducing discharge may justify revocation and court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier, by making an alteration in his 'descriptive list' so as to cause it to appear that his term of enlistment, which was in fact five years, was three years only, induced the regimental commander to give him an honorable discharge at the end of three years' service;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held, upon the fraud being presently discovered, that the discharge might legally be revoked and the soldier be brought to trial by court-martial under the ninety-ninth (now sixty-second) article of war. R. 21, 390, May, 1866.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI A 4. Discharge procured by fraudulent representation of civilian employment may be canceled and punished
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier secured his discharge by a fraudulent representation that he had secured a good position in civil life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held, that his arrest, trial, and punishment, and the cancellation of the discharge certificate were legal. C. 28879, Aug. 23, 1911; see also P. 49, 454, Oct. 16, 1891.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI B 1. Insane soldier's discharge ineffective; may be recalled and canceled
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who became insane while in the service was in hospital on account of the insanity at the expiration of his term of service. A discharge certificate was thereupon issued to him (in contravention of the Army Regulations covering such cases) and his discharge was noted on the records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held, that, being insane, his notice of discharge was ineffective to deprive him of the right to be sent to the Government Hospital for the Insane or to preclude the Government from recalling and canceling the discharge. Advised that the same be recalled and canceled, and the man committed to the Government Hospital in accordance with the regulations. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI B 2. Mental incapacity discovered after discharge without honor may lead to amendment to honorable discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier was discharged without honor and it was afterwards discovered that at the date of his discharge he was suffering from incipient dementia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held, that he was thus irresponsible for certain derelictions of duty. He was then honorably discharged and the records in the office of The Adjutant General were amended accordingly. C. 5897, Mar. 23, 1899.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI C 1. Correcting description of type of discharge on certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier was ordered discharged without honor, but was actually issued a dishonorable discharge;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held, that a new discharge certificate may be issued or the present one may be changed to show he was discharged 'without honor.' C. 7102, Oct. 5, 1899.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI C 2. Mitigation ambiguity — issued dishonorable should be recalled if inconsistent with mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewing authority mitigated a sentence which included dishonorable discharge and confinement as follows: 'Sentence is reduced to 18 months.' Through a belief that only the confinement portion of the sentence had been thus mitigated a dishonorable discharge was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the command issued by the reviewing authority could be interpreted only as a mitigation of the complete sentence to confinement to 18 months, even though the explanation was made that the word 'sentence' was through a clerical error written instead of 'confinement,' and further, held, that if a dishonorable discharge had been issued it should be recalled and canceled as void and inoperative under the terms of the mitigated sentence. C. 11211, Sept. 11, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI D. Executed discharge by competent authority vs. incompetence of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A legally executed discharge issued by competent authority cannot be revoked, but an executed discharge issued by incompetent authority is not binding upon the Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI D 1. Civil magistrate lacks authority to adjudicate military right to discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a United States commissioner in Indiana issued to a United States marshal a warrant for the arrest of a deserter from the Army, and, upon such deserter being brought before him, adjudicated the question of his right to discharge from the military service, and ordered him discharged therefrom,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the entire proceeding was coram non judice and a gross assumption and exceeding of authority, and advised that the facts be communicated to the Attorney General for his action, and that the deserter be forthwith rearrested and brought to trial by court-martial. P. 58, 287, Mar., 1893.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI E. Orders directing discharge may be revoked before taking effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that an order which directs a discharge may be revoked or suspended at any time before the discharge has actually taken effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI F. Revocation where discharge order not effectively delivered and cause ceases to exist
rubrics_metrics.description: An order was issued directing a discharge without honor of a soldier on account of his being in the hands of the civil authorities, serving sentence of imprisonment. The discharge had not been delivered actually or constructively when it developed that the soldier, after trial by jury, was acquitted and released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held, that the order directing his discharge should be revoked and the discharge certificate canceled, as the cause of the issuance of the discharge did not further exist and the discharge had not been effected. C. 10567, May 31, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI G. Unauthorized convening of general courts-martial renders sentences and discharges void
rubrics_metrics.description: Several soldiers were tried in the Department of the Dakota by a court-martial convened by a lieutenant colonel and sentenced to be dishonorably discharged. The sentence was approved by the lieutenant colonel commanding the department and the execution of such sentences was entered upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that as a lieutenant colonel in command of a department had no authority to convene a general court-martial that the sentences of such court were null and void and that the dishonorable discharges which had been executed pursuant to such sentences should be revoked. Held further that the men who were serving such illegal sentences should, after the revocation of the dishonorable discharges which had been issued to them, be brought to trial before a legally constituted court, discharged without honor, or restored to duty. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI G 1. Discharge pursuant to illegal sentence has no effect; soldier may be returned to duty
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a soldier who was dishonorably discharged pursuant to an illegal sentence,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that as the sentence was null and void the dishonorable discharge was of no effect and the soldier could be returned to duty without trial. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI G 2. Revocation of illegal dishonorable discharge restores prior status and allows trial before proper tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a soldier who, pursuant to an illegal sentence, was dishonorably discharged,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the dishonorable discharge was of no effect and that its revocation would place him in exactly the same status that he was in preceding his being brought to trial. Held further that he could be brought to trial before a legally constituted tribunal on the original charges. O. 16710, Feb. 29, 1908.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI G 3. Status after void sentence — may be discharged without honor as of delivery date
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier pursuant to an illegal sentence was dishonorably discharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the dishonorable discharge was of no effect and that his status was the same as it was preceding his trial and that he could be discharged without honor, as of the date when the discharge without honor was delivered, even though he had been confined in a military prison as a general prisoner. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI G 4. Temporary commanders lack authority to convene general courts-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: A colonel who was temporarily in command of the Army of Cuban Pacification issued orders purporting to convene general courts-martial. The officers designated met and tried cases and sentenced soldiers to dishonorable discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that as a colonel in command of an army has no authority to convene a court-martial all the sentences were null and void and the dishonorable discharges based upon them were of no effect and that the status of the men concerned was that of men awaiting trial under the original charges. (Citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI G 5. Sentencing by an illegal court composed of enlisted men is void
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier during the Civil War was tried by a court composed of enlisted men and sentenced to be drummed out of the service. Entry was made on the records that he was discharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that he had not been tried and that the so-called sentence was illegal, and the discharge, for that reason, inoperative. C. 2213, May 8, 1896.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVI II. Legislative private act may amend records but not authorize new discharge certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: A Lieutenant of the Forty-third New York Infantry was dropped in 1861 by order on account of absence without leave. Legislative relief was afforded in his case by means of a private act, which provided that he should hereafter be held and considered to have been honorably discharged from the military service of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that this act authorized a mutilation of the records and an entry on the old records, but that it did not authorize the issuance of an honorable discharge certificate. C. 17797, Apr. 12, 1905.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVII A. Executive cannot undo lawful dismissal by general court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer was lawfully separated from the military service by the legally approved sentence of a general court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that it was beyond the power of the Executive to grant an honorable discharge, to revoke the dismissal which had been fully executed, or to issue an instrument in the nature of a discharge certificate purporting to separate the applicant from the volunteer service in any other way than that determined by the approved sentence of the court-martial in his case. C. 23153, May 4, 1908.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVII B. Discharges under April 23, 1908 act for medical officers — timing of issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 of the act of April 23, 1908 (35 Stat. 67), provides that if the unfavorable finding of an examining board in the case of a medical officer is concurred in by the board of review, the officer reported disqualified for promotion shall, if a first lieutenant or captain, be honorably discharged from the service with one year's pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that in such a case the discharge should be issued on the date when the officer's failure to qualify was reported to the Secretary of War, or so soon thereafter as, by an exercise of reasonable diligence, a discharge certificate could be procured and forwarded to the officer whose connection with the military service it operates to sever. C. 23135, Dec. 11, 1909.

rubrics_metrics.name: XVIII A. Finality of dismissal of cadets once executed — only Congress can restore
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain cadets were dismissed by order of the Secretary of War, which order was approved by the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that as the dismissal of these cadets had been completely executed the President could not reconsider or revoke the order for their discharge or pardon them so as to restore them to their former status at the Military Academy, and that an act of Congress would be necessary. C. 29471, Aug. 24, and Oct. 16, 1909; similar holding re cadet discharged for disability, C. 25946, Dec. 11, 1909.

rubrics_metrics.name: XIX. Congressional act may authorize Secretary to amend rolls and issue certificate retroactively
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War may by an act of Congress be authorized and required to amend the rolls and records so as to show that a soldier was honorably discharged as of the date on which he was in fact dishonorably discharged, and give him a discharge certificate to that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: XX A. Presidential revocation of nomination may constitute discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: The President nominated a man as an officer in the Volunteer force during the Civil War. The Senate declined to confirm the appointment. The President then revoked the appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the revocation by the President amounted to a discharge from the service. C. 9096, Dec. 11, 1900.

rubrics_metrics.name: XX B. Presidential authority over Philippine Scouts separations limited as to punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that it is within the authority of the President to terminate the engagement of any officer or enlisted man of the Philippine Scouts by an honorable discharge whenever his services are no longer needed or when the public interest demands his separation from the military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further held that it is not within the power of the Executive to summarily dismiss an officer of the Philippine Scouts by way of punishment for an offense, as such separation from the service is expressly forbidden by section 1229, R. S., and the ninety-ninth article of war. C. 22129, Dec. 10, 1907.

rubrics_metrics.name: XX C. Department commander authority to summarily discharge undesirable soldiers in special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of six soldiers who had been imprisoned under sentence of a civil court, who were plainly undesirable as soldiers, and concerning whom it was clear that they should be summarily discharged as being an incubus to the service,
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the department commander had authority to order the discharge of these men without honor, as it was not one of the cases coming within that part of the regulations which requires the action of the Secretary of War. C. 23259, Jan. 14 and 19, 1909.

rubrics_metrics.name: XX D 1. Fourth article of war vests power in commanding general to determine discharge type in disability cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth article of war vests in the commanding officer of a department specific authority to discharge enlisted men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that there can be no doubt as to the authority of the commanding general of the department as an incident of his power to discharge, to determine from the report of the medical officer the nature of the discharge to be issued in each case in cases of disability. If the disability was contracted in the line of duty an honorable discharge issues. If, however, the disability is shown to be due to the vicious habits of the soldier, an honorable discharge cannot issue, and the separation of the soldier from the military service will be accomplished in the operation of a discharge without honor. C. 24131, Nov. 24, 1908.

rubrics_metrics.name: XX D 2. Limit on delegation of disability-discharge authority to district commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: The commanding officer, district of North Alaska, requested authority to discharge an enlisted man on surgeon's certificate of disability;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that under the fourth article of war he could not be given such authority. C. 6565, June 13, 1899. (Note re later act and General Order directing that orders for discharge on account of disability will not be issued except by the War Department.)

rubrics_metrics.name: XX E. Change of mind regarding reenlistment not basis for discharge without honor
rubrics_metrics.description: A Signal Corps soldier was under orders for service in the Philippines Division, and preceding his departure for those islands signed a written agreement that he would reenlist for further service in the islands. When the time approached for his discharge he declined to reenlist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the soldier had merely changed his mind, and that as an honest change of intention does not taint a soldier's character, his change of intention could not be used as a basis for granting him a discharge without honor, and recommended that power should not be given to the commanding general, Philippines Division, to grant discharges without honor in similar cases. C. 15581, Aug. 5, 1909.

rubrics_metrics.name: XX F. Court-martial sentencing limits as to types of discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that a court-martial cannot impose either an honorable discharge or a discharge without honor, nor can a dishonorable discharge be imposed except by sentence of court-martial.

rubrics_metrics.name: XXI A. Dismissal under special examination act treated as honorable discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of Volunteers was examined as to his qualifications by a board of officers under 'an act to provide for the examination of certain officers of the Army,' approved June 25, 1864, and was reported mentally disqualified for the duties of his office and was thereupon dismissed by Executive order in accordance with the provisions of the act;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that the dismissal was in effect an honorable discharge from the service. P. 46, 333, Apr., 1891; 65, 31, May, 1894.
